medium.title: Hardcoded password 'secure' for KeyStore in MainActivity
medium.description: The app uses a hardcoded password ('secure') to protect a secret key entry within a KeyStore. Because this password is hardcoded in the binary, an attacker who obtains the 'secretKeyStore' file from the device's external storage (e.g., via root access or physical extraction) can use this password to decrypt and recover the AES secret key.
medium.impact: An attacker who obtains the KeyStore file can use the hardcoded password to decrypt and retrieve the AES secret key.

lines_html: java.security.KeyStore keyStore = java.security.KeyStore.getInstance(java.security.KeyStore.getDefaultType());
keyStore.load(null, null);
java.security.KeyStore.ProtectionParameter pp = new java.security.KeyStore.PasswordProtection(new char[]{'s', 'e', 'c', 'u', 'r', 'e'});
keyStore.setEntry("SECRET_KEY", new java.security.KeyStore.SecretKeyEntry(secretKey), pp);
java.io.File file = new java.io.File(getExternalFilesDir(null), "secretKeyStore");
java.io.FileOutputStream fos = new java.io.FileOutputStream(file);
keyStore.store(fos, null);

medium.recommendation: Use the Android Keystore system to generate and store keys in a hardware-backed container, avoiding manual password protection with hardcoded strings.

medium.title: Sensitive KeyStore stored on external storage
medium.description: The application saves the KeyStore file containing a secret AES key to the external files directory using getExternalFilesDir().
medium.impact: Sensitive cryptographic material is stored in a location that is more accessible than internal storage, increasing the risk of exfiltration on older Android versions or rooted devices.

lines: result.setText("Successfully saved key in the keystore");
android.util.Log.d("Secure", "Successfully saved key in the keystore");
lines_html: java.security.KeyStore keyStore = java.security.KeyStore.getInstance(java.security.KeyStore.getDefaultType());
keyStore.load(null, null);

keyStore.setEntry("SECRET_KEY", new java.security.KeyStore.SecretKeyEntry(secretKey), pp);
java.io.File file = new java.io.File(getExternalFilesDir(null), "secretKeyStore");
java.io.FileOutputStream fos = new java.io.FileOutputStream(file);
keyStore.store(fos, null);
result.setText("Successfully saved key in the keystore");
android.util.Log.d("Secure", "Successfully saved key in the keystore");

medium.recommendation: Store sensitive data and cryptographic keys in the app's internal storage or, preferably, use the Android Keystore system.

info.title: Application is debuggable in this build
info.description: android:debuggable="true" lets any user with adb attach a debugger to the process, read and modify memory, and inspect application data. The application is marked as debuggable (android:debuggable="true"), which allows an attacker with physical or root access to attach a debugger to the process, inspect memory, and potentially bypass security controls.
info.impact: Full runtime access to the app's process and data on any device with adb.
info.recommendation: Remove android:debuggable or set it to "false" for release builds.

reasons: Debuggable release build. A debuggable build is a release-pipeline defect rather than an exploitable flaw - attaching a debugger already requires ADB access to the device. Worth fixing, not worth a severity.
Attaching a debugger requires ADB access, which is a release-pipeline defect rather than an exploitable vulnerability.

info.title: Lack of screen capture protection
info.description: The app does not set FLAG_SECURE in MainActivity, allowing the system to take screenshots or record the screen.
info.impact: Sensitive information displayed on the screen can be captured by other apps or the user.

lines_html: public class MainActivity extends android.support.v7.app.AppCompatActivity {
static javax.crypto.SecretKey secretKey = null;
@Override // android.support.v7.app.AppCompatActivity, android.support.v4.app.FragmentActivity, android.support.v4.app.SupportActivity, android.app.Activity
protected void onCreate(android.os.Bundle savedInstanceState) {
setContentView(edu.ksu.cs.benign.R.layout.activity_main);
android.widget.TextView result = (android.widget.TextView) findViewById(edu.ksu.cs.benign.R.id.result_text);

reasons: Screen contents not protected from capture. Without FLAG_SECURE, what a screen shows can end up in screenshots, screen recordings and the task-switcher preview. That matters on screens showing credentials, card numbers or balances; on its own it is a hardening note.
Screen contents not protected from capture reaches at most CVSS 3.3 (Low); the vector given scores this finding above anything the class does.
The lack of FLAG_SECURE is a hardening note unless a screen showing sensitive data is identified.

info.title: No network security config declared
info.description: The app declares neither android:networkSecurityConfig nor usesCleartextTraffic, so it relies on platform defaults and pins no domain. With targetSdkVersion 27 those defaults still permit cleartext HTTP (see the cleartext finding).
info.impact: Without pinning, anyone who gets a CA trusted on the device can read and alter the app's TLS traffic.
info.recommendation: Declare a network security config that disables cleartext and pins the domains that carry sensitive traffic.

reasons: No certificate pinning. Pinning defends against an attacker who already controls a trusted CA or the device's trust store. Without one of those, TLS is still doing its job. It becomes a finding when paired with what the unpinned channel actually carries.
The lack of certificate pinning is a hardening gap that only matters if the channel carries sensitive data.

info.title: targetSdkVersion 27 allows implicit component export
info.description: On targetSdk 27, any component with an intent-filter is exported unless it says otherwise.
info.recommendation: Raise targetSdkVersion to 31+ and declare android:exported explicitly on every filtered component.

reasons: Legacy platform behaviour from SDK levels. An SDK level is a statement about which platform defaults apply, not a defect. It is context for the findings that depend on those defaults - pair it with one of them.
The SDK level enables a platform default, but no specific exported component is identified as a vulnerability.
warnings: Implicit export only applies below targetSdk 31; confirm the app's targetSdkVersion before treating this as exploitable.

The configuration permits cleartext traffic, but no specific request is shown to be sent over HTTP.
warnings: Cleartext is blocked by default from targetSdk 28; confirm the declared target and any network security config.

info.title: Task hijacking (StrandHogg) possible on Android 10 and lower
info.description: minSdkVersion 22 lets the app run on Android versions before 11, and its task affinity is its package name "edu.ksu.cs.benign". There, another app can declare the same affinity, with allowTaskReparenting, and have its own activity shown in this app's task.
info.impact: On a device running Android 10 or lower, a malicious app can put a look-alike screen on top of this app's task, phishing credentials or keeping the real app from being shown.
info.recommendation: Raise minSdkVersion to 30, where Android fixed this. Until then, android:taskAffinity="" on the <application> mitigates the original attack, though not its runtime variant on unpatched Android 9 and lower.
